opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's something we thought about quite a bit.

In the original HippoRAG setup, the benchmarks we worked with, like MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and HotpotQA, mostly have fairly short passages, often Wikipedia paragraphs of a few hundred tokens. At that length you don't really need chunking. You can hand the whole passage to the LLM during offline indexing and ask it to do named entity recognition and then extract the triples, and it does a pretty good job of capturing the important relationships.

As passages get longer, things change. If you give a model a long document and ask for every meaningful triple, a few problems show up. First, recall drops. The model tends to grab the most salient facts and skip the detailed relationships buried in the middle, and those are often exactly what you need for multi-hop questions. Second, long passages contain more coreference, things like "he," "the company," or "this approach," and the model can lose track of who those refer to across a long span, so you get triples that are ambiguous or wrong. Third, there's the practical side: output length and cost, and a single extraction call that tries to do too much at once.

So with longer documents, chunking becomes pretty important, but you want to do it carefully. The chunks should be small enough that extraction stays dense and accurate, without being so small that you cut a relationship in half or lose the context needed to resolve an entity. Some overlap between chunks helps, and so does carrying a bit of document-level context, like the title or the main entities, into each chunk.

There's also a nice property on the graph side. Because HippoRAG links everything through shared entity nodes and synonymy edges, splitting a document into chunks doesn't break things the way it can in pure dense retrieval. Entities that show up in different chunks still get connected in the graph, and Personalized PageRank can walk across those connections. So chunking for extraction quality doesn't cost you as much global coherence as you might expect.

The short version: for short passages, chunking mostly doesn't matter. As passages get longer, it becomes a real lever on triple quality, and the graph structure helps you recover the cross-chunk connections afterward.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark passages were short and generally did not need chunking, but it does not state that they contained only two to four sentences.

r002.rationale: It describes missed details and coreference errors in long passages, but does not identify difficulty tracking where extracted triples originated within a passage.

r003.rationale: It mentions ambiguous or wrong triples from coreference, but does not identify hallucinated relations between different sentences as a risk.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a good question, and it's one of those things that sounds like an implementation detail but actually matters quite a bit for how the knowledge graph ends up looking.

So in HippoRAG, the way we build the index is that we take each passage and run it through what we call OpenIE, open information extraction, with an LLM. We first ask it to extract the named entities, and then we ask it to extract triples, subject-relation-object, grounded in those entities. Those triples become the nodes and edges of the graph, and that's what the Personalized PageRank step walks over at retrieval time.

Now, the datasets we evaluated on, things like MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, those are mostly built on Wikipedia paragraphs, so the passages are already pretty short, maybe a hundred, two hundred tokens. At that length we honestly didn't have to think about chunking much. The model can see the whole passage, keep track of all the entities, and produce a fairly complete set of triples.

But when you move to longer documents, and this is something we've heard a lot from people trying to apply HippoRAG to their own data, you start to see two failure modes if you don't chunk. The first is just recall. If you hand an LLM several thousand tokens and ask it to extract everything, it tends to get lazy. It'll pull out the most salient facts and quietly drop a lot of the long-tail relations, and those long-tail relations are often exactly the ones you need for a multi-hop question. The second is a kind of entity confusion, where the model starts mixing up which attribute belongs to which entity when there are many similar entities in the same context.

So chunking helps there, but it introduces its own tension. If your chunks are too small, you lose the context needed to resolve references. The passage says "he founded the company in 1998," and if the "he" was introduced three sentences earlier in a different chunk, you either get a triple with "he" as the subject, which is useless, or you get nothing. That's one reason the entity extraction step comes first and why we lean on the synonymy edges in the graph, so that even if two chunks refer to the same thing slightly differently, they get connected.

The way I'd put it is that passage length isn't really the variable you care about directly. What you care about is whether a chunk is a coherent unit of meaning that the LLM can fully attend to. For most text, something in the range of a few hundred tokens with sentence-aware boundaries works well. For longer documents, I'd rather over-chunk and rely on the graph to stitch things back together than under-chunk and lose facts at extraction time, because once a triple isn't extracted, there's no retrieval mechanism that can recover it later.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark passages were short (about 100–200 tokens) and needed little chunking, but it does not state that they contained two to four sentences.

r002.rationale: It describes entity confusion and lost context across chunks, but not difficulty tracking where extracted triples originated within a longer passage.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify hallucinated relations between different sentences as a risk.

astra-6.text:
I think the longer the passage gets, the more useful chunking becomes, because you’re asking the model to identify entities and extract relationships across more text in a single call. With a short passage, you can often process it directly. With a much longer passage, even if it fits in the context window, you may start missing relationships or extracting them less consistently.

But there’s a tradeoff: if you make the chunks too small, you can separate an entity from the context needed to understand its relationships. So I’d think of chunking as a way to balance extraction coverage with enough local context. In HippoRAG, the graph can connect information extracted from different chunks, but it still depends on those relationships being captured correctly in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response does not state that benchmark passages had two to four sentences or that chunking was unnecessary; it says short passages can often be processed directly.

r002.rationale: It mentions missing relationships or inconsistent extraction, but not difficulty tracking where extracted triples originated.

r003.rationale: It warns that small chunks can separate entities from context, but does not identify hallucinated relations between sentences as a risk.

sol-6.1.text: I think passage length matters quite a bit, because as a passage gets longer, you're asking the model to identify more entities and extract more relationships in a single call. It can miss things, and those missing triples affect what you can retrieve later. So for relatively short passages, you may not need additional chunking. For longer documents, chunking becomes more useful to keep the extraction manageable and thorough. The tradeoff is that if you make the chunks too small, you can lose the context needed to understand a relationship, especially when it spans sentences. So you want chunks that preserve enough context without overwhelming the extraction step.
